claims.text: The initial materials are single-phase FCC equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and selected quaternary or ternary subsets produced by thermomechanical processing.
Annealing at approximately 700°C for 1, 5, or 10 hours can create systematically differing degrees of chemical short-range order.
Rapid quenching preserves the chemical short-range order induced during annealing.
The relevant structural mediator is local chemical short-range order on the nanometer scale.
Increasing chemical short-range order creates local energy barriers.
The local energy barriers associated with chemical short-range order enhance dislocation nucleation.
The local energy barriers associated with chemical short-range order pin dislocations or impede their motion.
Coherent chemical-short-range-order features act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Greater chemical short-range order raises yield strength.
Greater chemical short-range order modifies strain-hardening behavior.
Lower chemical short-range order produces a more homogeneous matrix with fewer obstacles to dislocation motion.
Lower chemical short-range order results in lower strength.
Lower chemical short-range order results in higher ductility.
Relative to the untreated equiatomic quinary baseline, samples with greater chemical short-range order will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the untreated equiatomic quinary baseline, samples with greater chemical short-range order will exhibit a changed strain-hardening rate.
The proposed relationship applies within single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys subjected to the specified thermomechanical and annealing conditions.
Synchrotron X-ray diffraction or neutron scattering can quantify the induced chemical short-range order through diffuse-scattering or related ordering parameters.
